newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan cabinet agency targets 6.7 pct '98 GDP rise.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan cabinet agency targets 6.7 pct '98 GDP rise.

text.p: The Council for Economic Planning and Development, the Taiwan cabinet's top economic planner, said on Wednesday the island's gross domestic product should grow an annual 6.7 percent in 1998, state radio said.

If achieved, such growth would be sharply higher even than the 6.24 percent official target for 1997 -- and fully one percentage point above the Taiwan economy's disappointing 5.71 percent performance in 1996.
"Next year's economy will be even better than this year," the radio quoted the council as saying.
Details were not immediately available.

It was not immediately known whether the new 1998 target reflected this week's sharp depreciation of the Taiwan dollar, which analysts say will spur exports -- Taiwan's economic lifeblood and a major component of GDP.
The local unit, facing intense selling pressure since late on Monday, closed at T$28.480 on Wednesday against Tuesday's already sharply depreciated T$28.170 finish.

While official, targets set by the Council on Economic Planning and Development, typically have been somewhat more bullish than forecasts issued by the Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics.
In May, directorate chief Wei Duan has issued his agency's initial forecast for 1998 growth at 6.26 percent.
Taiwan's economy has been experiencing a gathering economic recovery, but analysts are divided about its pace and breadth.
GDP growth spiked to an annual 6.62 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996 and an even better 6.83 percent in the first quarter of 1997, raising hopes that the recovery was in place.

In May, the statistics agency forecast second-quarter growth slipping to 5.61 percent, reflecting cyclical factors and a farm epidemic that halted pork exports -- a US$1.55 billion industry -- and caused significant losses in the meatpacking sector.
The brightest spot in Taiwan's economy has been its stock market, where the index has more than doubled since a March 1996 military crisis with rival China in the Taiwan strait.
Electronics have replaced financials as the driving force.

While many analysts are optimistic about the stock market's 1997 prospects, some worry that its spectacular rise may be coming at the expense of other sectors -- chiefly the bond and money markets as well as the long-depressed property market.
Economics minister Wang Chih-kang on July 22 expressed confidence that the 6.24 percent growth target would be met, citing growth of both investment and and industrial output.
In June, industrial output rose 5.28 percent compared to June 1996, and export orders rose an annual 6.01 percent.
Wang said first-quarter private investment rose 8.95 percent year-on-year and was seen rising 11.54 percent for all of 1997 to mark Taiwan's best performance in recent five years.
Private economists have been less sanguine, saying Taiwan's heavy and increasing reliance on high-technology exports could leave the island exposed if that or other sectors sag.

Economists say political factors -- a cabinet reshuffle and congress of the ruling Nationalist Party in August, President Lee Teng-hui's September visit to Central America and local elections in December -- could add stress to the economy.
China's Communist Party congress in October could raise acute uncertainty in Taiwan, seen by Beijing as a rebel-held province that must be retaken since a 1949 civil war split.
There have been reports that Beijing will accelerate its schedule for Taiwan's "reunification with the motherland", which could rattle the island's hypersensitive financial markets.
